title: Hyperparameter Optimization at Scale
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Hyperparameter Optimization at Scale ##### 11 days of compute to find nothing A team in Noida ran a grid search over a gradient boosting model: 4 learning rates × 3 tree depths × 3 subsample values × 3 regularisation values = 108 configurations, each taking about 2.5 hours across 5-fold CV. Total: 270 compute-hours, roughly ₹1.1 lakh on their cloud contract, spread over 11 days. The best configuration beat their hand-picked baseline by 0.4%. The postmortem found two things. Seventy of the 108 runs were visibly worse than the baseline within the first fold and still ran to completion — nobody had implemented pruning. And subsample and regularisation barely affected the metric at all, so nine of every twelve runs were re-testing the same two meaningful dimensions with different irrelevant values. A 40-trial Optuna study with median pruning reproduced the best result in 22 compute-hours. Hyperparameter optimisation is not "try lots of things". It is a sequential decision problem under a compute budget, and treating it as one is worth an order of magnitude. ##### Grid, random and Bayesian **Grid search** evaluates the Cartesian product. Its failure is dimensional: six hyperparameters at four values each is 4,096 trials. Bergstra and Bengio's classic result explains why this is worse than it looks. When only 2 of 6 dimensions matter, a grid of 4,096 trials tests each important dimension at only **4 distinct values**, while 60 random trials test them at **60 distinct values each**. The grid spends its entire budget on combinations of parameters that do not affect the outcome. ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt rng = np.random.default_rng(42) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5)) # Grid: 25 points, but only 5 unique values on each axis g = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 5) gx, gy = np.meshgrid(g, g) axes[0].scatter(gx.ravel(), gy.ravel(), s=60) axes[0].set_title("Grid: 25 trials, 5 unique values per dimension") # Random: 25 points, 25 unique values on each axis axes[1].scatter(rng.random(25), rng.random(25), s=60, color="#e53e3e") axes[1].set_title("Random: 25 trials, 25 unique values per dimension") for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel("important parameter"); ax.set_ylabel("irrelevant parameter") fig.tight_layout() ``` **Random search** samples independently from distributions. Embarrassingly parallel, handles mixed continuous and categorical spaces, and a genuinely strong baseline. Its weakness is that it never learns — trial 300 is as uninformed as trial 1. **Bayesian optimisation** builds a probabilistic model of the objective from completed trials and uses it to choose the next point. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Evaluate a few random trials] --> B[Fit a surrogate model:
score = f hyperparameters] B --> C[Acquisition function scores
every candidate point] C --> D[Pick the candidate maximising
expected improvement] D --> E[Run the trial - the expensive part] E --> F[Add the result to history] F --> B ``` The intelligence lives in the **acquisition function**. Expected Improvement balances two things: regions where the surrogate predicts a high score (exploitation) and regions where the surrogate is uncertain (exploration). Pure exploitation gets stuck in a local optimum; pure exploration is random search. EI does both automatically, and it is why 40 informed trials can beat 400 random ones. ##### TPE and Optuna Optuna's default sampler is the **Tree-structured Parzen Estimator**, which inverts the usual Bayesian formulation. Rather than modelling `p(score | params)` with a Gaussian process, TPE splits completed trials into a "good" set (top γ fraction, typically 25%) and a "bad" set, fits a density `l(x)` to each, and samples points maximising the ratio `l(x)/g(x)` — "likely under good trials, unlikely under bad ones". Two consequences. It scales far better than a GP to high dimensions and mixed parameter types. And it handles **conditional** search spaces naturally, which a GP cannot. ```python import optuna import lightgbm as lgb import numpy as np from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING) def objective(trial: optuna.Trial) -> float: params = { "objective": "binary", "verbosity": -1, "n_estimators": 3000, # log=True for anything spanning orders of magnitude "learning_rate": trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 5e-3, 0.3, log=True), "num_leaves": trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 15, 255, log=True), "min_child_samples": trial.suggest_int("min_child_samples", 5, 200, log=True), "subsample": trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.5, 1.0), "subsample_freq": 1, "colsample_bytree": trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.4, 1.0), "reg_alpha": trial.suggest_float("reg_alpha", 1e-8, 10.0, log=True), "reg_lambda": trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 1e-8, 10.0, log=True), } # CONDITIONAL space — this is TPE's structural advantage over a grid params["boosting_type"] = trial.suggest_categorical("boosting_type", ["gbdt", "dart"]) if params["boosting_type"] == "dart": params["drop_rate"] = trial.suggest_float("drop_rate", 0.05, 0.3) params["skip_drop"] = trial.suggest_float("skip_drop", 0.3, 0.7) cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) scores = [] for fold, (tr, va) in enumerate(cv.split(X, y)): model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**params) model.fit(X.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr], eval_set=[(X.iloc[va], y.iloc[va])], eval_metric="average_precision", callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100, verbose=False)]) p = model.predict_proba(X.iloc[va])[:, 1] scores.append(average_precision_score(y.iloc[va], p)) # Report an intermediate value so the pruner can act trial.report(float(np.mean(scores)), step=fold) if trial.should_prune(): raise optuna.TrialPruned() trial.set_user_attr("fold_std", float(np.std(scores))) trial.set_user_attr("best_iteration", int(model.best_iteration_)) return float(np.mean(scores)) study = optuna.create_study( direction="maximize", study_name="fraud_lgbm_v3", storage="sqlite:///optuna.db", # use PostgreSQL for parallel workers load_if_exists=True, sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=42, n_startup_trials=20, multivariate=True, group=True), pruner=optuna.pruners.MedianPruner(n_startup_trials=10, n_warmup_steps=2), ) study.optimize(objective, n_trials=200, timeout=6 * 3600, show_progress_bar=True) ``` Five design decisions in that code, each worth understanding: **`log=True`** for scale-spanning parameters. Learning rate 0.001 → 0.01 is the same *relative* jump as 0.01 → 0.1. Uniform sampling would put 90% of samples in the top decade. **`n_startup_trials=20`** controls how long TPE samples randomly before modelling. Too few and the surrogate is built on noise. **`multivariate=True`** lets TPE model parameter interactions rather than treating each dimension independently — usually a clear improvement. **Persistent storage** turns the study into a resumable, shareable, analysable object. Kill the process and `load_if_exists=True` picks up where it stopped. **Conditional parameters** — `drop_rate` simply does not exist in gbdt trials. The search space is defined by Python control flow, which grid search cannot express. ##### Pruning and multi-fidelity Pruning kills trials that are clearly losing, freeing compute for promising ones. This is where the Noida team's 12× saving came from. | Pruner | Rule | Best for | |---|---|---| | `MedianPruner` | Prune if below the median of prior trials at this step | Safe default | | `SuccessiveHalvingPruner` | ASHA: allocate in rungs, promote the top 1/η | Massively parallel | | `HyperbandPruner` | Runs SHA across multiple budget schedules | Unknown budget/quality trade-off | | `PercentilePruner` | Configurable percentile threshold | Tuning aggressiveness | | `PatientPruner` | Wraps another, adds patience | Noisy learning curves | **Successive halving** is the core idea: start N configurations with a small budget, keep the top 1/η, give survivors η× more budget, repeat. ``` Rung 0: 81 configs × 1 unit of budget → keep 27 Rung 1: 27 configs × 3 units → keep 9 Rung 2: 9 configs × 9 units → keep 3 Rung 3: 3 configs × 27 units → keep 1 ``` Total budget: 324 units for what would cost 2,187 units at full budget for all 81. **Hyperband** wraps SHA in an outer loop over different initial budgets, hedging against the failure mode where a slow-starting configuration is the eventual winner. That is a real risk when comparing learning rates — a low rate looks bad early and wins late. ```python study = optuna.create_study( direction="maximize", pruner=optuna.pruners.HyperbandPruner(min_resource=1, max_resource=10, reduction_factor=3), ) ``` The parameter that catches people: **`n_warmup_steps` must be high enough to survive early instability.** Set it too low and you prune every configuration that uses a learning-rate warmup or needs a few folds to stabilise. Pruning is most valuable when the objective produces meaningful intermediate values — training epochs, cross-validation folds, or increasing subsample sizes. On a single-fit objective with no intermediate signal, there is nothing to prune. ##### Designing the search space The space matters more than the sampler, and this is where most of the human judgement lives. ```python def objective(trial): # GOOD: log scale for multiplicative parameters lr = trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-3, 0.3, log=True) # GOOD: ranges wide enough that the optimum is interior leaves = trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 15, 511, log=True) # GOOD: step for parameters where fine granularity is meaningless depth = trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 3, 12, step=1) # GOOD: categorical for genuinely discrete choices booster = trial.suggest_categorical("booster", ["gbtree", "dart"]) # BAD: too narrow — the optimum will sit on the boundary # bad_lr = trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 0.09, 0.11) # BAD: uniform on a multiplicative parameter # bad_reg = trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 0.0, 10.0) ``` Three rules. **Check whether the best trial's parameters sit on a boundary** — if they do, your range was too narrow and you should widen it and rerun. **Use log scale** for learning rates, regularisation strengths, and anything else where the meaningful unit is a ratio. And **prune the space between studies** using importance analysis, which is exactly what the Noida team never did: ```python importances = optuna.importance.get_param_importances(study) for k, v in importances.items(): print(f"{k:22s} {v:.4f}") # learning_rate 0.4821 # num_leaves 0.2934 # min_child_samples 0.1102 # colsample_bytree 0.0621 # subsample 0.0288 <- barely matters # reg_alpha 0.0134 <- barely matters # reg_lambda 0.0100 <- barely matters ``` Fix the bottom three at sensible defaults and rerun with the budget concentrated on the top three. That single step typically doubles the effective trial count. ##### Parallel and distributed tuning Because Optuna stores trials in a database, distribution is nearly trivial: run the same script on N workers pointing at the same storage. ```bash # Any number of workers, any machines, same command for i in $(seq 1 8); do python tune.py --study-name fraud_lgbm_v3 \ --storage postgresql://optuna@db:5432/optuna \ --n-trials 25 & done wait ``` ```python # In-process parallelism study.optimize(objective, n_trials=200, n_jobs=4) ``` Use **PostgreSQL or MySQL** for real parallelism — SQLite locks under concurrent writes and will corrupt a long study. On Kubernetes, run workers as a `Job` with `parallelism: 8`. One subtlety worth knowing: with 8 concurrent workers, TPE proposes trials before seeing the other 7 results, so the sequential advantage shrinks. Beyond roughly 16 workers, **ASHA-style pruning contributes more than sampler intelligence** — at that point you are effectively running a smart random search with aggressive early termination, which is fine. Ray Tune is the alternative when you need fault-tolerant scheduling, GPU-aware placement or population-based training. Optuna is simpler and integrates with Ray if you want TPE inside Ray's scheduler. ##### Analysing the study The output is not just `best_params`. ```python print(f"best value: {study.best_value:.5f}") print(f"best trial: {study.best_trial.number}") print(f"pruned: {sum(t.state == optuna.trial.TrialState.PRUNED for t in study.trials)}") print(f"complete: {sum(t.state == optuna.trial.TrialState.COMPLETE for t in study.trials)}") import optuna.visualization as vis vis.plot_optimization_history(study).show() # still improving, or plateaued? vis.plot_param_importances(study).show() vis.plot_slice(study).show() # marginal effect per parameter vis.plot_contour(study, params=["learning_rate", "num_leaves"]).show() vis.plot_parallel_coordinate(study).show() vis.plot_intermediate_values(study).show() # see pruning in action import pandas as pd df = study.trials_dataframe() top = df.nlargest(10, "value")[["number", "value", "params_learning_rate", "params_num_leaves", "user_attrs_fold_std"]] print(top.round(5)) ``` Four things to read from those outputs. **Optimization history still climbing at trial 200** means you stopped too early. **Parameter importances** tell you what to drop from the next study. **The top-10 table with fold standard deviation** matters more than people realise. If the best trial has a high `fold_std`, you may have optimised into noise — prefer a configuration in a broad stable region over a lone spike. **The gap between `best_value` and test performance** is real and expected. `best_value` is optimistically biased because you selected on it across 200 trials. Report the final number on a test set the study never touched. ##### Multi-objective optimisation Production models trade off accuracy against latency, size and cost. Optimising a weighted sum forces you to pick the weights before you know the trade-off curve. ```python def objective(trial): n_leaves = trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 15, 511, log=True) n_trees = trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 100, 2000, log=True) model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(num_leaves=n_leaves, n_estimators=n_trees, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, verbose=-1) model.fit(X_train, y_train) auc = average_precision_score(y_val, model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]) latency_ms = measure_p99_latency(model, X_val, n=500) return auc, latency_ms study = optuna.create_study( directions=["maximize", "minimize"], sampler=optuna.samplers.NSGAIISampler(seed=42), ) study.optimize(objective, n_trials=300) for t in study.best_trials: # the Pareto front print(f"AP {t.values[0]:.4f} p99 {t.values[1]:6.1f}ms {t.params}") vis.plot_pareto_front(study, target_names=["PR-AUC", "p99 latency (ms)"]).show() ``` The **Pareto front** is the set of configurations where you cannot improve one objective without worsening another. Handing a stakeholder a front — "0.341 at 40 ms, or 0.348 at 190 ms" — is a far better conversation than handing them one number. Note that pruning does not apply to multi-objective studies, and NSGA-II needs more trials than TPE because it is an evolutionary method. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Need to tune] --> B{How many parameters?} B -->|1-2| C[Grid search is fine] B -->|3+| D{Objective has intermediate values?} D -->|Yes: epochs or CV folds| E[Optuna TPE + MedianPruner] D -->|No| F[Optuna TPE, no pruner] E --> G{Budget large, many workers?} G -->|Yes| H[Hyperband + PostgreSQL storage] G -->|No| I[Sequential TPE] F --> I H --> J[Analyse: history, importances, top-10 stability] I --> J J --> K{Still improving? Boundary hits?} K -->|Yes| L[Widen ranges, more trials] K -->|No| M[Report on untouched test set] ``` ##### Common mistakes - Grid search in more than three dimensions. - Uniform sampling of learning rate or regularisation instead of log-uniform. - No pruner, so hopeless trials consume the entire budget. - `n_warmup_steps` too low, pruning every configuration that needs a few folds. - SQLite storage with parallel workers. - Ranges too narrow, so the optimum sits on a boundary and nobody notices. - Ignoring `plot_param_importances` and re-tuning irrelevant parameters forever. - Reporting `best_value` as the final performance. - Selecting a lone spike with high fold variance over a broad stable region. - Spending 300 trials on hyperparameters when one new feature would have moved the metric more. ##### Hands-on Tune a gradient boosting model with Optuna using a well-designed search space and median pruning, then run an equivalent-budget grid search and compare best score, wall-clock time and trial count. Report how many trials the pruner terminated early. Then run `get_param_importances`, identify the two parameters that actually mattered, and rerun with the space narrowed to those — comparing the result at the same budget is the exercise that makes the lesson concrete. For the mini-project, build a reusable Optuna tuning framework: a config-driven search space with at least one conditional parameter, pluggable sampler and pruner, database storage supporting resume and parallel workers, logging of every trial with user attributes, and a report function producing the optimisation history, parameter importances and slice plots. Add multi-objective support returning `(metric, latency)` and produce a Pareto front. Test it on two different model families to prove it is genuinely reusable, and include a section on how you chose the search-space ranges — that reasoning is the part that transfers. For the assignment, explain why Bayesian optimisation is more sample-efficient than grid search, and describe what pruning saves. Cover the surrogate model, the acquisition function's exploration-exploitation balance, and Bergstra and Bengio's dimensional argument — then quantify the pruning saving with your own numbers. ##### Key takeaways - Grid search wastes budget re-testing dimensions that do not matter; random is a strong baseline and Bayesian is better. - TPE models densities of good versus bad trials, which scales to high dimensions and handles conditional spaces naturally. - Pruning is usually the largest single speedup available — report intermediate values and let it kill losers early. - Log-scale your multiplicative parameters, widen ranges until the optimum is interior, and prune the space by importance. - The study's real output is understanding: history, importances, and the stability of the top configurations — not just `best_params`.

practical_task_reference: Use Optuna to tune a gradient boosting model with a well-designed search space, enable pruning to stop weak trials early, and compare the best result and time to a grid search.
mini_project_reference: Build a reusable Optuna tuning framework for a model that defines a conditional search space, uses pruning, runs trials in parallel, logs all trials, and visualizes the optimization history and parameter importances.
assignment_reference: Explain why Bayesian optimization is more sample-efficient than grid search, and describe what pruning saves.
